The time horizon for evaluation corresponds to the duration of the study. Treatment Side-Effects and Complications 7. A complication is defined as a condition or event that negatively impacts a patient’s health, causing irreversible damage or necessitating a change in therapeutic approach, such as prolonged hospitalization. 8. Side effects are unwanted symptoms caused by treatment, which are usually temporary and resolve spontaneously. 9. These terms are often used interchangeably, but they differ in severity and implications. Major Infections (Grade II+) 10. Post-operative infections of the genital tract requiring antibiotics and/or hospitalization are considered major infections. 11. Systemic symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting, and dehydration, while local symptoms include foul-smelling discharge and pain. 12. Consequences may include hospitalization, antibiotic therapy, loss of workdays, psychological harm, and long-term sequelae such as infertility or chronic pelvic inflammatory disease. 13. Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical history and follow-up assessments, but may also involve blood tests, ultrasound, or culture/sensitivity testing. 14. Minor infections causing mild symptoms are often indistinguishable from side effects and are not typically considered. 15. Major infections are distinguished by additional signs such as foul-smelling discharge, fever, tenderness, or severe pain. 16. Treatment involves hospitalization, antibiotics, and rehydration, depending on severity. 17. Recovery typically occurs within a few days to a few weeks. Major Bleeding (Grade II+) 18. Post-operative bleeding requiring intervention, such as vaginal packing or cervical sutures, is classified as major bleeding. 19. Symptoms include vaginal bleeding, often with clots, and may be accompanied by hypotension and shock-related symptoms like weakness, dizziness, vomiting, or loss of consciousness. 20. Consequences can include shock, death in severe cases, anemia, psychological harm, and loss of workdays. 21. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, examination, and routine blood tests. 22. Major bleeding is distinguished from minor bleeding by the presence of clots, significant drops in blood pressure or hemoglobin levels, or the need for intervention. 23. Treatment may involve hospitalization, vaginal packing, antibiotics, and management of shock. In rare cases, surgical interventions like hysterectomy may be required. 24. Recovery depends on severity, but bleeding usually stops within a few days. Procedure-Associated Pain 25. Pain and lower abdominal cramps may occur during or immediately after the procedure. 26. Consequences include the need for medications, psychological harm, and loss of workdays. 27. Pain is assessed through patient feedback using visual scales and evaluation by the treatment provider. 28. Pain exceeding mild, tolerable levels or typical menstrual pain is considered significant. 29. Treatment involves analgesics based on the severity of the pain. 30. Pain typically resolves within one week after the procedure. Cervical Stenosis 31. Cervical stenosis is defined as the narrowing of the endocervical canal to the extent that a cotton swab or uterine sound (3 mm diameter) cannot be introduced. 32. Symptoms may include dysmenorrhea (rare) or hematocolpos. 33. Consequences include dysmenorrhea, reduced fertility (though evidence is inconsistent), and difficulty obtaining endocervical samples during screening or colposcopic assessment. 34. Diagnosis is made through clinical examination. 35. Treatment may involve cervical dilation. 36. The condition may persist for up to three years. Spontaneous Abortions 37. Spontaneous abortion, or miscarriage, is defined as the loss of a clinically recognized pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation or the expulsion of an embryo or fetus weighing 500 g or less. 38. Symptoms include spotting, bleeding, pain, and passage of fleshy material through the vagina. 39. Consequences include pregnancy loss, hospitalization, psychological harm, and loss of workdays. 40. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, examination, and ultrasound, though patient-reported cases may be less reliable. 41. Treatment may involve bed rest, hospitalization, tocolytic medications, or evacuation in cases of incomplete abortion. Premature Rupture of Membranes (PROM) 42. PROM is defined as the rupture of membranes before the onset of labor at any gestational age. 43. Symptoms include watery vaginal discharge in later gestational stages without other signs of labor. 44. Consequences include preterm labor, low birth weight, perinatal death, hospitalization, cesarean section, and psychological harm. 45. Diagnosis is made through clinical examination, ultrasound, and tests to detect amniotic fluid. 46. Treatment may involve bed rest, fetal monitoring, induction of labor, or cesarean section. Preterm Birth 47. Preterm birth is defined as delivery before 37 weeks of pregnancy, with early preterm birth occurring before 32 weeks. 48. Consequences include hospitalization, tocolytics, cesarean section, low birth weight, perinatal loss, and psychological harm. 49. Gestational age is best determined by ultrasound but may also be assessed clinically or self-reported. 50. Treatment options include vaginal delivery or cesarean section. Perinatal Deaths 51. Perinatal death refers to death occurring between 22 completed weeks of gestation and 7 days after birth. 52. Consequences are not applicable. 53. Assessment is based on standardized definitions from medical providers or individual reports, though the latter may lack confirmation. Infertility 54. Infertility is defined as the inability of women of reproductive age (15–49 years) to conceive after 12 months or more of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse. 55. Consequences include the inability to achieve pregnancy. 56. Assessment is based on self-reported data. 57. Treatment options aim to improve the chances of conception. Stigmatization 58. Stigma is a mark of disgrace associated with a particular circumstance or quality, often involving stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination. 59. Symptoms include fear, avoidance, depression, and other psychological effects. 60. Consequences include social and psychological harm, such as isolation, intimate partner abuse, negative self-image, and altered health-seeking behavior. 61. Assessment may involve qualitative methods, surveys, or scales to measure stigma. 62. Treatment includes community education and support for affected individuals. Increased Viral Shedding in Women Living with HIV 63. Increased viral shedding refers to the detection of HIV RNA in the genital tract of women living with HIV, regardless of plasma viral load levels. 64. Consequences include the potential transmission of HIV to non-infected partners. 65. Assessment involves mRNA-based viral load detection from vaginal fluid. Acceptability of Screening and Treatment 66. Acceptability refers to the extent to which women, providers, or program managers consider a screening test or treatment intervention appropriate based on cognitive and emotional responses. 67. Consequences include better compliance with future screening, improved community acceptance, and enhanced service provision. 68. Assessment involves questionnaires evaluating side effects, satisfaction, and willingness to recommend services. Screening Test Performance 69. Positive predictive value (PPV) measures the proportion of true positive cases among those who test positive, reflecting the accuracy of the screening test. 70. Sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive value (NPV) are ideal but rarely reported in screen-and-treat studies. Reduction in Cervical Cancer Incidence and Mortality 71. Reduction in incidence refers to a decrease in newly diagnosed cervical cancer cases over time. 72. Reduction in mortality refers to a decrease in deaths from cervical cancer following treatment. Unnecessary Interventions or Overtreatment 73. Unnecessary interventions include colposcopy and biopsy for false-positive results, as well as overtreatment of lesions unlikely to progress.
